name: Beth Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government. What you say is confidential. What does an ordinary day at your accounting firm involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am Beth, 27, and I lead a team preparing accounts and tax returns. I have a master’s degree and a chartered accountancy qualification, and I start with the returns that need a client call before checking the rest. I enjoy turning a confusing tax letter into a short explanation, but the train commute eats my evenings.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are you placed financially, and how do you use technology?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My pay is higher than usual for this work and I have eight months of expenses saved. Malik, my partner, and I rent together, and there are plenty of accounting firms nearby. I use AI now and then for internal meeting outlines, but I remove client details and check each draft against my notes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds like the little office changes I am used to. Nobody has cancelled the tax deadline because a tool drafts faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell clients the return still gets a human check, even if the team uses a faster way to sort receipts. My team would keep its usual client calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, this is a quiet picture. I earn above the usual accountant salary, have eight months of expenses saved, and there are many firms nearby; the real annoyance is a long commute.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep using AI now and then to outline internal meeting notes, with no client data in it. Each month I would add a set amount from salary to my travel savings, then use the first year to keep serving the same tax clients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about my job and income. The train delay is more likely to spoil Tuesday than this kind of software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you check in the note outline?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I compare action dates and names with my handwritten notes before sending anything. If a draft invents a task, it goes in the bin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the travel savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want to visit my parents across the country without using emergency money. The monthly transfer is new cash from pay, not a plan to spend the eight-month reserve.

say: I would tell clients **human checks** remain on every return.
I would keep our usual **client calls** while receipt sorting gets a little faster.
think: Eight months of savings and **higher pay** make my own income feel safe.
The **long commute** bothers me more than this small software change.
do: Keep checked **meeting outlines** free of private client figures.
Transfer a fixed **salary amount** to a travel account monthly.
feel: I feel **calm** about work and money.
S0.quote: If a draft invents a task, it goes in the bin.
fieldNote: She already uses AI **occasionally** for internal notes and checks dates against handwriting.
Strong savings and abundant local firms support a **calm** response, while her commute remains a mundane irritation.

steps.text: Keep serving tax clients with checked internal note outlines
Transfer fixed monthly salary amount into travel savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This would show up in return drafts and client questions first. The firm could change the work before changing anyone’s title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues that we need a clear list of which tax checks the software does and how missed errors are recorded. I would ask management to use some saved time for client meetings rather than quietly raise file targets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my own team lead hours might hold, but the firm could stop replacing junior accountants and then expect me to cover their files. If fees fall enough, even my well-paid role could be trimmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask my manager Colin for paid training on the firm's approved review tool, and take the class if it is offered. In the first year I would test it on old returns with personal details removed, record missed deductions, and bring those results to the monthly workload meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because a new target could turn a good job into too many files and fewer hours. Eight months of cash gives me a choice, but it does not keep a team intact.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want in the workload meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would bring the number of errors caught per hour alongside the number of files completed. Speed by itself makes a bad target when a client can face a penalty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave if targets rise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if a posted senior vacancy at another firm offers a salary that still covers my rent and commuting costs. Plenty of firms are nearby, but I would wait for a written offer before resigning.

say: I would ask for **error records** and a clear list of automated tax checks.
I would put **quality measures** beside file targets in workload meetings.
think: Unfilled **junior posts** could leave me covering many more files each week.
Falling client fees might still trim my **well-paid hours** despite my savings.
do: Take **paid review-tool training** if Colin offers the approved class.
Test anonymised **old returns** and bring missed deductions to workload meetings.
Move only for a **written senior offer** covering rent and commuting.
feel: I feel **anxious** about hours and workload despite my reserve.
S1.quote: Speed by itself makes a bad target when a client can face a penalty.
fieldNote: She looks for **error rates**, not only file volume, before accepting new targets.
Her willingness to change firms is **conditional** on a written offer and adequate salary.

steps.text: Take paid approved review-tool class if offered
Bring anonymised error results to monthly workload meeting
Accept written senior offer covering rent and commute if targets rise

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is hard to square with a client book built slowly. I would need the firm to tell us what it still expects to sell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AGI taking accounts and tax preparation in 2028 requires a straight answer about client responsibility and staff pay. Robots arriving around 2031 do not give this screen job a later deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect the firm to cut preparation fees and perhaps my whole team. My eight-month reserve would let me look carefully, but I would be losing a high salary and could not assume nearby firms were hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From this month I would divert a new portion of salary into a separate job-loss fund and stop planning the long-haul holiday with my partner Malik. If my post ends in the first year after 2028, I would apply for a published-salary tax appeals vacancy and take an offer only if the pay covers our fixed bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because I expect the income I built my life around to vanish. I have time to search, but two years could go quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Malik about the trip?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my partner Malik we are keeping the weekend visit to my parents but postponing the expensive flight abroad. We would leave the eight-month reserve untouched while I keep earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a new degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, a full degree would spend the job-loss fund before it helps. I would enrol in a short tax appeals course only if the firm paid the fee and gave me paid study time.

say: I would ask for **client responsibility** and staff pay plans before 2028.
I would say robots around **2031** cannot postpone a tax desk shock in 2028.
think: The firm may cut my **whole team** and its preparation fees.
My eight-month reserve helps, but replacing a **high salary** may be hard.
do: Transfer new **salary savings** into a job-loss fund and postpone the long-haul holiday.
Enrol in a **tax appeals course** only with paid fees and study time.
Apply only for **appeals vacancies** with pay covering fixed bills after job loss.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by a likely loss of high income.
S2.quote: I expect the income I built my life around to vanish.
fieldNote: She expects the **2028 desk change** to hit before capable robots arrive around 2031.
The holiday delay and new savings protect cash; retraining requires **paid fees** and study time.

steps.text: Transfer a new monthly salary portion into job-loss savings
Enrol in short appeals course only with paid fee and study time
Apply for published-salary appeals roles if job ends and pay covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years would make the training calendar possible. I could test a different part of accounting while the current clients still pay us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the firm should publish a five-year plan for junior training and tax dispute work. AGI hits our screen tasks in 2031, and robots around 2034 do not extend the life of routine returns.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still expect the fee base to shrink, but I could spend several years learning tax disputes while keeping my salary. I have enough saved to reject a poor offer rather than rush into the first vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would complete the professional body's paid tax disputes module using my training allowance and ask Colin to assign one supervised appeal each quarter. In the first year after 2031 I would move to a salaried appeals post only if one is advertised; otherwise I would keep my existing clients as long as they pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy because the work still changes, but five years lets me try real cases before deciding. I can see a path without giving up my current income early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the training allowance cover?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The firm gives senior staff a fixed course budget, and the module fee fits inside it. I would enrol this winter and show Colin the case exercises before asking for appeals work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you decide on a vacancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the written salary with our rent and my current pay. A role called appeals specialist would not be worth a large cut just because the title sounds safer.

say: I would ask for a **five-year plan** covering juniors and dispute work.
I would name **2031** as the account-desk date, before robots around 2034.
think: Routine preparation **fees** may shrink even if clients still need explanations.
A funded **course allowance** and actual appeals cases give me another path before I leave.
do: Complete the **funded disputes module** and take supervised quarterly appeals only if Colin assigns them.
Keep serving **existing clients** while their work pays if no appeals vacancy opens.
Move after **2031** only after comparing written salary with rent and current pay, rejecting large cuts.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, with time to test cases and compare salaries.
S3.quote: A role called appeals specialist would not be worth a large cut just because the title sounds safer.
fieldNote: Unlike a vague funding request, she has an existing **course allowance** and a module fee that fits it.
She still needs **assigned cases** and an advertised salary before treating appeals as a secure new role.

steps.text: Complete tax disputes module using existing course allowance this winter
Take one supervised appeal quarterly if Colin assigns it
Take advertised appeals post after 2031 only after written salary comparison rules out a large cut
Keep existing tax clients while their work pays if no appeals vacancy opens

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade would let me see whether appeal work actually grows. I would not need to turn a guess into next year’s rent decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell friends that account preparation faces AGI in 2036 while robots come around 2039. Firms have ten years to keep training staff and tell clients who signs the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect routine tax fees to fall by 2036, but I could have a strong client appeals record by 37. My savings and local options give me room, though I would still need written terms before leaving a good job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep serving my tax clients now, complete one approved client appeals case each quarter if Colin assigns it, and put a fixed part of salary into a reserve each month. In the first year after 2036, if preparation work contracts, I would accept a posted appeals role only with a written salary high enough for our rent and fixed costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the trade I trained for changing, but not trapped. A decade could give me proof of what clients still need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change your housing plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Malik and I would keep the current rental until an appeals salary is in writing. We would not sign a larger lease on the promise that client work will be safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the firm to protect?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask Colin to keep supervised trainee cases each year, so new staff learn to question a wrong figure. A fast answer still needs someone who knows what a wrong answer looks like.

say: I would separate **2036 accounts work** from robots arriving around 2039.
I would ask Colin to protect **supervised trainee cases** each year.
think: Routine tax **fees** may fall even with a decade of preparation.
Savings, nearby firms, and real **appeals cases** could give me choices.
do: Serve existing **tax clients** and take appeals cases only if assigned.
Transfer a fixed **salary portion** into a reserve each month.
Accept a **posted appeals role** after 2036 only with written salary covering rent and fixed costs.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, but not trapped by the time horizon.
S4.quote: A fast answer still needs someone who knows what a wrong answer looks like.
fieldNote: She uses the decade to accumulate **assigned appeals cases**, not just a new title.
Her housing and job decisions require a **written salary** that covers rent and fixed costs.

steps.text: Keep serving tax clients and take appeals cases only if assigned
Transfer fixed salary portion into reserve each month
Accept posted appeals job after 2036 only with written salary covering rent and fixed costs

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my team and high salary could disappear together. A clear staffing plan, funded time to learn appeals, and an income bridge after a cut would help. I would still need an advertised vacancy with a salary that pays our fixed bills.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask what the firm will count as good work after the tool arrives. If my firm counts only files finished, my firm may miss the errors that cost clients money. I would want the error record beside every speed target.

headlineQuote: If my firm counts only files finished, my firm may miss the errors that cost clients money.
portrait: Beth is a **27-year-old** team lead with a master’s degree and chartered qualification who prepares accounts and tax returns.
She has **higher pay**, eight months saved, a partner, and many nearby firms.
She uses **AI occasionally** for internal notes, removing client details and checking drafts against handwriting.
She pushes for **error measures** beside file targets and takes a funded appeals module.
The **2028** shock alarms her; later dates allow assigned cases and reserve building before any salaried move.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her team and high salary before she finds another role.
whatWouldHelp: She wants a clear **staffing plan**, funded appeals training, an income bridge, and advertised roles paying fixed bills.
